analysis.one_liner: Bars any federal money from being spent to carry out the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to six House committees and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited every federal dollar from being obligated or spent to carry out any part of the Affordable Care Act or the health-related provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law. That would have stopped the law's insurance subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and consumer protections from being put in place. The bill was sent to six committees, moved no further, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the concentrated interests that bore costs under the health law: high-income households facing the law's Medicare surtaxes and the tax on high-cost employer plans, and insurers and other industries subject to the law's fees. It would also have saved general taxpayers the cost of the law's spending, while stripping coverage expansion and consumer protections from millions of ordinary people.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and industries taxed by the law

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all federal funds from being obligated or expended to carry out any provision of the Affordable Care Act or the health-related provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law [S2][S3].
Would have halted spending on the law's insurance subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and related implementation programs, eliminating their cost to the Treasury [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on people who stood to gain coverage under the law — the uninsured, people with preexisting conditions, and those relying on the law's subsidies and Medicaid expansion — who would have lost those benefits with nothing to replace them [S2].

drawbacks.text: Defunding the law would have cut off its subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and consumer protections — including coverage guarantees for people with preexisting conditions — without replacing them, leaving the law's mandates and taxes legally in place while its benefits went unspent [S2][S3].
The bill is a two-sentence funding prohibition with no substitute plan, so even supporters of scaling back the law acknowledged it addressed no specific cost or provision [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no replacement for the programs it would have defunded, so its only benefit was ending the law's spending while leaving millions of people without the coverage and protections the law provided. It was a blunt repeal-by-attrition measure rather than a targeted fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by one member, referred to six House committees, and never advanced to a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Connie Mack of Florida introduced the bill on June 28, 2012 [S1].

It was referred to six full committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and House Administration — and then to subcommittees, where it sat without any markup or vote through the end of the 112th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, Affordable Care Act implementation continued: the people the law covered through subsidies and Medicaid expansion kept those benefits, and the health industries gaining new insured customers kept their new markets. Supporters of full repeal gained only a symbolic roll-call-free record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA enrollees and the coverage expansion's beneficiaries

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 28, 2012, and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the only recorded support was a single House Republican sponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: Defunding the law would have stripped away the subsidies and mandates that route millions of new paying customers through private insurers. Ordinary people would have lost coverage at the same time insurers lost the market, so their interests here ran together.

The law's Medicare surtax on high earners and the tax on high-cost employer plans fell on upper-income households; defunding implementation would have spared them those costs while ordinary people lost the coverage benefits funded by them.

Providers had gained from expanded coverage — hospitals in particular benefited from fewer uninsured patients — and would have lost that with defunding, though some also faced Medicare payment reductions under the law.
